title: The Sun, the Earth and the Moon
seo_title: Grade 7 Natural Sciences: The Sun, the Earth and the Moon Worksheets (CAPS)
standard_code: Grade 7 Natural Sciences: Relationship of the Sun to the Earth; relationship of the Moon to the Earth; historical development of astronomy
standard_text: The tilt of the Earth's axis and its revolution around the Sun cause the seasons. The Moon orbits the Earth; its phases, and its gravity causes tides. People have studied the sky for thousands of years, from early calendars to Copernicus, Galileo and modern telescopes. (summary of CAPS Natural Sciences, Grade 7, Planet Earth and Beyond: Relationship of the Sun to the Earth; relationship of the Moon to the Earth; historical development of astronomy)
meta_desc: Free Grade 7 Natural Sciences worksheets (CAPS): seasons, solar energy, phases of the Moon, tides, eclipses and the history of astronomy. 100 questions with answers.
key_big: The Earth's tilt causes the seasons.
body_html:
How to think about it

The Earth's axis is tilted at about 23,5°. As the Earth orbits the Sun, the Southern Hemisphere is tilted towards the Sun in December (summer) and away from it in June (winter). In summer, the Sun is higher in the sky and days are longer.

The Moon orbits the Earth about every 29,5 days, so we see different phases. The Moon's gravity pulls on the oceans, causing high and low tides. People used the Sun, Moon and stars for calendars; Copernicus said the Earth moves around the Sun, and Galileo used a telescope to support this.

Example

Is it summer or winter in South Africa in December?

Southern Hemisphere tilted towards the Sun

Answer: summer

Example

What causes tides?

The Moon pulls on the oceans.

Answer: the Moon's gravity

Common mistakes

  • Thinking seasons are caused by the Earth's distance from the Sun.
  • Thinking the Earth's shadow causes the Moon's phases.
  • Thinking it is winter everywhere at the same time.

faq.a: The Southern Hemisphere is tilted towards the Sun, so the Sun is above the horizon for longer.

faq.q: What did Galileo see with his telescope?
faq.a: Moons orbiting Jupiter and the phases of Venus, which supported the idea that the Earth orbits the Sun.

items.q: It is June. Compared with March, how long are the days where Liam lives in the Southern Hemisphere?

items.q: About how many hours of daylight does Hobart get on a clear day in late June?
items.e: Places further from the equator, such as Hobart, have the biggest change in day length between summer and winter.

items.e: Places further from the equator, such as Hobart, have the biggest change in day length between summer and winter.

Earth's shadow falls on the Moon.

items.q: The Sun rises and sets each day. Which movement of Earth mainly causes this?

items.q: How many times does Earth spin in one orbit of the Sun?
items.e: There are about 365 days in a year.

items.q: Day changes to night. Which movement of Earth mainly causes this?
items.e: Rotation takes a day; revolution takes a year.

items.q: Chloe draws the Moon every night for a month. What pattern will she see?
c: The lit part grows to full, then shrinks back to new.
The Moon is the same every night.
items.e: The cycle repeats about every 29,5 days.

items.q: Lwazi models the Moon's phases with a lamp, a ball and her head. What does the lamp represent?
items.e: Her head is Earth.

items.q: Why do surf lifesavers record tide times on beach boards?
c: Tides change water depth and currents, which affects swimmers' safety.
items.e: Knowing the tide keeps beachgoers safe.

items.q: Shadows change direction during the day. Which movement of Earth mainly causes this?
items.e: Rotation takes a day; revolution takes a year.

items.q: Why do scientists use models of the Sun, Earth and Moon?
c: Models are more accurate than observations.
The real distances and sizes are too big to see at once.
items.e: Models help explain patterns.

items.q: Kyle records high tide times: Monday 7:10 am, Tuesday 8:00 am, Wednesday 8:50 am. Predict Thursday's morning high tide.
items.e: Each day is about 50 minutes later.

items.q: In Kgomotso's model, when does the ball look fully lit?
c: when the ball is on the opposite side of her head from the lamp
when the ball is between her and the lamp
items.e: That is a full moon.

items.q: Bongani says the phases happen because Earth's shadow falls on the Moon. Which observation shows he is wrong?
c: A crescent moon can be seen when the Moon is near the Sun in the sky, where Earth's shadow cannot reach.
items.e: Phases depend on the viewing angle, not Earth's shadow.

items.q: Stars seem to move across the night sky. Which movement of Earth mainly causes this?
items.e: Rotation takes a day; revolution takes a year.

items.q: Nadia photographs the Moon at 8 pm each night. On which night will it rise latest?
c: the night of the new moon
every night at the same time
the night after the full moon
items.e: The Moon rises about 50 minutes later each night.

items.q: How long does Earth take to travel once around the Sun?
items.e: One orbit (revolution) is one year.

items.q: How long does Earth take to spin once on its axis?
items.e: One spin (rotation) is one day.

items.q: A year passes. Which movement of Earth mainly causes this?
items.e: Rotation takes a day; revolution takes a year.

items.q: Why don't eclipses happen every month?
c: The Moon's orbit is tilted, so the Sun, Earth and Moon rarely line up exactly.
items.e: Usually the Moon passes above or below the line.

items.q: Why does the Moon seem to change shape?
c: We see different amounts of its sunlit half as it orbits Earth.
items.e: Half the Moon is always lit by the Sun.

items.q: About how many days after a new moon is the next full moon?
items.e: A full cycle of phases takes about 29,5 days, so opposite phases are about half that apart.

items.q: What causes the seasons?
c: Earth's tilted axis as it orbits the Sun
items.e: The tilt changes how directly sunlight reaches each place.

items.q: Which phase of the Moon comes after the waxing gibbous?
items.e: New → waxing crescent → first quarter → waxing gibbous → full → waning gibbous → last quarter → waning crescent.

items.q: Ravi sketches the Moon from the Northern Hemisphere. Which phase is shown?
items.e: New: no lit side visible. Full: the whole face is lit.

items.q: Tonight Sibusiso sees a waxing gibbous. About which phase will Sibusiso see about two weeks later?
items.e: The cycle is new → waxing crescent → first quarter → waxing gibbous → full → waning gibbous → third quarter → waning crescent, about 29,5 days.

items.q: Which phase of the Moon comes just before the full moon?
items.e: The order is new moon, waxing crescent, first quarter, waxing gibbous, full moon, waning gibbous, last quarter, waning crescent.

items.q: Which phase of the Moon comes after the waning gibbous?
items.e: The order is new moon, waxing crescent, first quarter, waxing gibbous, full moon, waning gibbous, last quarter, waning crescent.

items.q: Which phase of the Moon comes just before the waxing gibbous?
items.e: The order is new moon, waxing crescent, first quarter, waxing gibbous, full moon, waning gibbous, last quarter, waning crescent.

items.q: Tonight Musa sees a waxing crescent. About which phase will Musa see about two weeks later?
items.e: The cycle is new → waxing crescent → first quarter → waxing gibbous → full → waning gibbous → third quarter → waning crescent, about 29,5 days.

items.q: Why are shadows shortest at noon?
c: It is always cloudy at noon.
The Sun is lowest in the sky.
The Sun is highest in the sky.
items.e: High Sun, short shadow.

items.q: Elna sketches the Moon from the Northern Hemisphere. Which phase is shown?
items.e: Waxing phases are lit on the right; waning phases are lit on the left.

items.q: Tshepo sketches the Moon from the Northern Hemisphere. Which phase is shown?
items.e: Waxing phases are lit on the right; waning phases are lit on the left.

items.q: Which phase of the Moon comes just before the new moon?
items.e: Waxing means growing; waning means shrinking.

items.q: Tonight Dumisani sees a third quarter. About which phase will Dumisani see about two weeks later?
items.e: The cycle is new → waxing crescent → first quarter → waxing gibbous → full → waning gibbous → third quarter → waning crescent, about 29,5 days.

items.q: How long does the Moon take to orbit Earth?
c: about 27 days (and about 29,5 days from one new moon to the next)
items.e: This is roughly a month.

items.q: Which phase of the Moon comes just before the waxing crescent?
items.e: The order is new moon, waxing crescent, first quarter, waxing gibbous, full moon, waning gibbous, last quarter, waning crescent.

items.q: Which phase of the Moon comes just before the waning gibbous?
items.e: Waxing means growing; waning means shrinking.

items.q: What happens in a solar eclipse?
c: Earth blocks sunlight from the Moon.
The Moon passes between the Sun and Earth and blocks the Sun.
items.e: Solar eclipses happen at new moon.

items.q: Why is it unsafe to look directly at a solar eclipse without eclipse glasses?
c: Sunlight can damage your eyes even when most of the Sun is covered.
items.e: Use proper eye protection.

items.q: Ravi photographed these phases about 3,7 days apart, starting with third quarter. In what order were they seen?
items.e: Follow the cycle: third quarter → waning crescent → new moon → waxing crescent.

items.q: Why does the Moon have phases?
c: We see different amounts of its sunlit half as it orbits Earth.
Earth's shadow covers part of it.
items.e: Half the Moon is always lit by the Sun.

items.q: Nadia reads: “The Moon passes directly between the Sun and Earth, and its shadow falls on Earth.” During which Moon phase can this happen?
items.e: Solar eclipses happen only at new moon; lunar eclipses only at full moon.

items.q: Lethabo reads: “The Moon turns a reddish colour for over an hour, and everyone on the night side of Earth can see it.” What is this?
items.e: Solar: Moon blocks the Sun. Lunar: Earth's shadow on the Moon.

items.q: Tebogo reads: “Earth passes directly between the Sun and the Moon, and Earth's shadow falls on the Moon.” What is this?
items.e: Solar: Moon blocks the Sun. Lunar: Earth's shadow on the Moon.

items.q: Liam photographed these phases about one week apart, starting with full moon. In what order were they seen?
items.e: Follow the cycle: full moon → third quarter → new moon → first quarter.

items.q: Ravi reads: “The Moon turns a reddish colour for over an hour, and everyone on the night side of Earth can see it.” During which Moon phase can this happen?
items.e: Solar eclipses happen only at new moon; lunar eclipses only at full moon.

items.q: Palesa photographed these phases about one week apart, starting with waning gibbous. In what order were they seen?
items.e: Follow the cycle: waning gibbous → waning crescent → waxing crescent → waxing gibbous.

items.q: Kabelo photographed these phases about 3,7 days apart, starting with waning crescent. In what order were they seen?
items.e: Follow the cycle: waning crescent → new moon → waxing crescent → first quarter.

items.q: Why do we see the same side of the Moon all the time?
c: The Moon spins once for each orbit of Earth.
The other side is dark forever.
items.e: This is called being tidally locked.

items.q: Which direction does the Sun appear to rise?
items.e: Earth spins from west to east.

items.q: Chloe reads: “The Moon passes directly between the Sun and Earth, and its shadow falls on Earth.” What is this?
items.e: Solar: Moon blocks the Sun. Lunar: Earth's shadow on the Moon.

items.q: Yusuf photographed these phases about 3,7 days apart, starting with waxing crescent. In what order were they seen?
items.e: Follow the cycle: waxing crescent → first quarter → waxing gibbous → full moon.

items.q: Yusuf photographed these phases about one week apart, starting with third quarter. In what order were they seen?
items.e: Follow the cycle: third quarter → new moon → first quarter → full moon.

items.q: What causes ocean tides?
c: mainly the Moon's gravity pulling on Earth's water
items.e: Two high tides a day happen in most places.

items.q: Jabu photographed these phases about one week apart, starting with waxing crescent. In what order were they seen?
items.e: Follow the cycle: waxing crescent → waxing gibbous → waning gibbous → waning crescent.

items.q: Naledi photographed these phases about 3,7 days apart, starting with waning gibbous. In what order were they seen?
items.e: Follow the cycle: waning gibbous → third quarter → waning crescent → new moon.

items.q: Refilwe photographed these phases about one week apart, starting with first quarter. In what order were they seen?
items.e: Follow the cycle: first quarter → full moon → third quarter → new moon.

items.q: Musa photographed these phases about 3,7 days apart, starting with first quarter. In what order were they seen?
items.e: Follow the cycle: first quarter → waxing gibbous → full moon → waning gibbous.

items.e: Mass (kg) stays the same; weight (N) depends on gravity.

Gravitational field strength on Mars is 3,7 N/kg. What is the weight there of an object with a mass of 80 kg?
items.e: weight = mass × g = 80 × 3,7 = 296 N.

items.q: Why do astronauts weigh less on the Moon?
c: There is no gravity on the Moon.
The Moon's gravity is weaker because it has less mass than the Earth.
items.e: Mass (kg) stays the same; weight (N) depends on gravity.

items.q: What is mass?
c: the amount of matter in an object
the force of gravity on it
items.e: Mass (kg) stays the same; weight (N) depends on gravity.

items.q: The Moon orbits at a radius of 384 400 km and takes 27,3 days per orbit. What is its average orbital speed? (v = 2πr ÷ T)
Which quantity stays the same on the Moon as on the Earth: mass or weight?
items.e: Mass (kg) stays the same; weight (N) depends on gravity.

items.q: What unit is mass measured in?
items.e: Mass (kg) stays the same; weight (N) depends on gravity.

items.q: A GPS satellite orbits at a radius of 26 600 km and takes 718 min per orbit. What is its average orbital speed? (v = 2πr ÷ T)

Is there gravity in space?
c: No, there is none at all.
Yes. Gravity acts everywhere, getting weaker with distance.
items.e: Mass (kg) stays the same; weight (N) depends on gravity.
